text:
Abstract  
Comparative assessments of public sequence repositories inform data availability and choice of resources for microbial genomics. We queried the NCBI GEO Series database and the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) via BRC Analytics to quantify holdings for Staphylococcus aureus. GEO was queried for Series (“GSE”) entries filtered by organism, returning a total of 500 series records. ENA was queried by NCBI taxonomy ID (1280), returning 181 408 sequencing run records. Both calls were limited to one record to obtain total counts from the metadata. The results indicate that ENA holds ~362-fold more raw sequencing runs than GEO Series records for S. aureus. GEO provides curated experiment descriptions and links to processed data files, whereas ENA delivers raw read data with standardized metadata and download URLs. These findings matter for researchers choosing between repositories for sequence retrieval, with GEO suited to transcriptomic and metadata-rich studies and ENA to raw-read–based analyses.

I. Introduction  
Background. Staphylococcus aureus is a clinically significant bacterial pathogen. Public repositories host complementary data: GEO archives processed expression and experimental series, ENA archives raw sequencing runs.  
Literature Review. No literature was retrieved for this query.  
Knowledge Gap. The relative scale of GEO and ENA holdings for S. aureus has not been quantified.  
Objective & Hypothesis. Objective: quantify and compare the total number of S. aureus records in GEO Series and ENA. We hypothesize that ENA holds substantially more raw sequencing runs than GEO holds Series entries.

II. Materials and Methods  
Study Design. We performed two independent metadata queries to quantify holdings.  
Materials.  
– GEO Series database accessed via NCBI E-utilities (tool: geo_search).  
– ENA via BRC Analytics proxy (tool: brc_ena_runs).  
Procedures.  
1. Call geo_search with arguments {"organism":"Staphylococcus aureus","term":"","entry_type":"gse","max_results":1} to obtain total Series count.  
2. Call brc_ena_runs with arguments {"taxonomy_id":"1280","limit":1,"offset":0} to obtain total run count.  
Statistical Analysis. Total counts were taken directly from the "total_count" field for GEO and "total_in_ena" for ENA. No further processing was applied.

III. Results  
Data Presentation.  
Table 1: Comparison of GEO and ENA Holdings for Staphylococcus aureus

| Resource | Data Type                      | Count    |
|----------|--------------------------------|---------:|
| GEO      | Series records (GSE)           |      500 |
| ENA      | Sequencing runs (fastq entries)| 181 408 |

Findings. GEO holds 500 Series records for Staphylococcus aureus. ENA holds 181 408 sequencing runs for the same organism.

IV. Discussion  
Interpretation. The ENA repository contains 181 408 raw sequencing runs, 362 times the number of GEO Series entries (500) for Staphylococcus aureus.  
Context. GEO Series provide curated experiment metadata and processed data links [1], while ENA delivers raw-read datasets with download URLs [2].  
Limitations. GEO’s “total_count” reflects only Series entries and excludes GSM, GPL, and GDS types; processed expression matrices are not directly accessible via the API. ENA’s “total_in_ena” counts runs regardless of platform or study type and may include overlapping replicates. Neither query assessed data quality, experimental design, or redundancy.  
Conclusion & Future Directions. ENA offers a broader set of raw sequencing data for S. aureus, while GEO offers focused experimental series with processed data metadata. Future work could stratify ENA holdings by library strategy and GEO by experiment type to guide specific use cases.

References  
[1] NCBI E-utilities esearch for GEO Series: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi  
[2] BRC Analytics ENA runs API for taxonomy 1280: https://brc-analytics.org/api/v1/ena/taxonomy/1280  

Acknowledgments  
Data were provided by the National Center for Biotechnology Information (GEO) and by BRC Analytics via the European Nucleotide Archive.
